label: Overthinking & anxiety
title: Bhagavad Gita on Overthinking: 7 Verses to Calm the Mind
description: Seven verses for a mind that won't switch off, starting with Arjuna admitting his own mind is as hard to hold as the wind (6.34). Sanskrit, plain English and one thing to try.
h1: Bhagavad Gita on overthinking: 7 verses to calm the mind
subtitle: For the 2 a.m. replay. Read one a night, or all seven right now.
keywords: how to control the mind bhagavad gita
intro: Arjuna said it first: the mind is restless, stubborn and as hard to hold as the wind (6.34). Krishna agrees, then teaches him what to do with it. The first two verses name the loop and where it starts. The next two give the mind somewhere to rest. Two more are practice you can start tonight. The last comes from the Mahabharata, from a woman who slept once she stopped waiting.

image.alt: A young woman lying awake at night while a diya beside her burns with a perfectly still flame
image.altGlobal: A young woman lying awake at night while a candle beside her burns with a perfectly still flame

days.heading: Even Arjuna couldn't hold his mind
days.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
days.forYou: Arjuna says this, and he was the finest archer of his time. He admits his own mind won't obey him. If yours keeps replaying the same conversation at 2 a.m., you are in good company, and the Gita takes the problem seriously before it offers anything.
days.today: Notice one loop today and name it to yourself: there it is again.

days.heading: How one thought carries you off
days.line: When the mind follows a wandering sense, it is swept off like a boat in the wind.
days.forYou: Krishna's picture is a boat with no one at the oar. One thought pulls, the mind follows, and judgement goes with it. Overthinking usually starts small, with one detail you keep going back to.
days.today: When you catch yourself drifting, ask what the first thought was.

days.heading: A lamp where there is no wind
days.line: Like a lamp in a windless place that doesn't flicker: that's a settled mind.
days.forYou: Krishna describes a flame that stays upright. It still burns and still gives light, and the wind around it makes no difference. You can have that steadiness too, for a few minutes at first.
days.today: Sit for two minutes and picture a flame that doesn't move. Come back to it whenever the mind runs.

days.heading: Little by little
days.line: Little by little, with patience and steady resolve, settle the mind and let other thoughts go.
days.forYou: The Sanskrit says śanaiḥ śanaiḥ: slowly, slowly. Nobody quiets a racing mind in one evening, and Krishna asks for patience with yourself while it settles.
days.today: Pick one small window today, like the walk to the car or the kettle boiling, and spend it with no input at all.

days.heading: Practice, and letting go
days.line: Yes, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But practice and letting go can train it.
days.forYou: Krishna's answer has two parts. Abhyāsa means coming back to the practice again and again. Vairāgya means loosening your grip on what the mind keeps chasing. You need both, because practice alone can turn into one more thing to worry about.
days.today: Choose one thing you keep replaying. Decide what you'll do about it and when, write it down, and set it aside until then.

days.heading: Bring it back. Again.
days.line: Wherever the restless mind wanders, gently bring it back. Again and again.
days.forYou: This verse expects the mind to wander. Krishna asks you to bring it back each time it does, gently, without scolding yourself. Every return counts as practice.
days.today: Tonight, each time a thought pulls you away from sleep, come back to your breath. Count the returns if it helps.

days.heading: The night she stopped waiting

story.title: Pingala's song
story.body: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira about Pingala, who sat awake one night waiting for a lover who never came. Every sound outside might have been his footsteps, so she kept listening. Late in the night she saw what was keeping her awake. It was her hope that someone else would arrive and settle her. She let that hope go, and she slept peacefully.
story.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.

days.forYou: A lot of overthinking is waiting in disguise: for a reply, a result, an apology. Pingala still cared. She stopped making her rest depend on it.
days.today: Name the one thing you're waiting on. For tonight, let it stay unanswered.

verse.sanskrit: सुखं निराशः स्वपिति नैराश्यं परमं सुखम् । आशामनाशां कृत्वा हि सुखं स्वपिति पिङ्गला ॥
verse.line: Pingala let go of her expectation and slept peacefully. Letting go of expectation is the greatest ease.

faq.q: What does the Bhagavad Gita say about overthinking?
faq.a: The clearest passage is 6.33 to 6.36. Arjuna says the mind is as hard to control as the wind, and Krishna agrees, then says it can be trained through practice (abhyāsa) and letting go (vairāgya). Chapter 2 (2.62 to 2.67) explains how dwelling on one thing grows into attachment and carries judgement away.

faq.q: Which Gita verse helps most with a racing mind?
faq.a: Many readers start with 6.35 (the mind can be trained), 6.26 (bring it back each time it wanders) and 6.19 (a lamp in a windless place). This plan uses all three, with 6.34 first so the problem is named before the answer.

faq.q: Can reading the Gita replace help for anxiety?
faq.a: No. These verses can steady you, but if worry is affecting your sleep, work or health for weeks, please talk to a doctor or counsellor. Reading the Gita and getting help go well together.
